name: Hittite

ancestors.notes: Hittite is the earliest-attested Anatolian language, split from Proto-Indo-European before the other branches (Hoffner & Melchert 2024).

notes: Skeleton. Extinct Anatolian (Indo-European) language of the Hittite Empire (c. 1650-1180 BCE), written in a form of Peripheral Akkadian cuneiform adapted from Northern Syria; the syllabic cuneiform signs are conventionally rendered in the standard Hittitological Latin transliteration scored here, following Assyriological practice as in akk.json. ⟨š⟩=/ʃ/, ⟨ḫ⟩ a laryngeal reconstructed as uvular fricative /χ/ (Kloekhorst 2008), macron marks vowel length. Doubled consonants ⟨pp tt kk ss šš ḫḫ⟩ intervocalically contrast with single-letter ⟨p t k s⟩; this is a genuine orthographic contrast, not a cartesian artifact, but its phonetic interpretation is debated in the literature — the traditional view (Melchert 1994, cited via Hoffner & Melchert 2024) reads it as a fortis/lenis (historically voiceless/voiced) contrast, while Wikipedia (Hittite language) notes Hittite scribes used the etymologically voiced and voiceless Akkadian cuneiform signs interchangeably, which some scholars instead take as evidence for a pure consonant-length distinction; scored here as a length/gemination contrast (doubled = long) without committing to the fortis/lenis phonetic story. Syllabic cuneiform sign-boundaries, plene (double vowel) writing, and word-internal sign polyphony are not modeled; a substantial PER floor is expected given the reconstructive nature of the transliteration.

sources.author: Hoffner, Harry A.; Melchert, H. Craig
